SAGES guidelines for laparoscopy during pregnancy (2017)
McGory et al., J Am Coll Surg (2007)

related.why: Taking the history of acute right iliac fossa pain
Consent for appendicectomy in a patient with particular needs

brief.scenario: Mrs Nadia Kershaw, 29, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has had 18 hours of right-sided abdominal pain, nausea and a temperature of 38.1°C. The examiner will give you further findings.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on her assessment and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Mother first, image to confirm, then operate without delay, with obstetrics alongside.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Delaying surgery because she is pregnant: perforation is the bigger risk to the baby.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess and resuscitate her with ABCDE, in left lateral tilt, and call obstetrics."

grid.label: Mother first
grid.fail: Focuses on the fetus before assessing and resuscitating the mother.
grid.pass: ABCDE of the mother first, in left lateral tilt; IV access, fluids, analgesia, antiemetic; early obstetric involvement.
grid.high: Explains fetal wellbeing depends on maternal perfusion, and a supine gravid uterus compresses the vena cava.

grid.label: Differential diagnosis
grid.fail: Diagnoses or excludes appendicitis on symptoms and signs alone.
grid.pass: Signs are less reliable in pregnancy; considers pyelonephritis, ovarian torsion, placental abruption and preterm labour; urine and pregnancy-adjusted bloods.
grid.high: Notes clinical scores are less accurate in pregnancy because white cells and nausea are often raised anyway, so imaging is needed.

grid.label: Imaging
grid.fail: Requests CT first, or refuses any imaging because she is pregnant.
grid.pass: Graded compression ultrasound first; MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive and available.
grid.high: CT is acceptable in an emergency when MRI is unavailable and the result will change management; discusses with a radiologist.

grid.label: Decision to operate
grid.fail: Delays surgery until after delivery, or treats with antibiotics alone.
grid.pass: Confirmed appendicitis needs appendicectomy without delay; non-operative treatment is not recommended in pregnancy.
grid.high: A short in-hospital period of observation with repeat ultrasound is acceptable when equivocal; delay to perforation is the greater danger.

grid.label: Operative approach
grid.fail: Says laparoscopy is contraindicated in pregnancy.
grid.pass: Laparoscopic appendicectomy is safe in any trimester where expertise exists; left lateral tilt; port entry adjusted to fundal height.
grid.high: Insufflation at 10–15 mmHg adjusted to her physiology; mechanical thromboprophylaxis and early mobilisation.

grid.label: Fetal risk
grid.fail: Cannot state the risks to the pregnancy, or quotes one fixed figure without context.
grid.pass: Fetal loss and preterm delivery, both higher with complicated (perforated) appendicitis.
grid.high: Fetal loss about 2% with simple, 4% with a negative operation and 6% with complicated appendicitis: accurate diagnosis matters both ways.

grid.label: Team and fetal monitoring
grid.fail: Operates without involving obstetrics or anaesthesia.
grid.pass: Obstetric and anaesthetic involvement; fetal heart documented (Doppler) before and after surgery; consent covers risks to the pregnancy.
grid.high: No prophylactic tocolytics: obstetrics treats signs of preterm labour; senior surgeon involved; documents the shared plan.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd get a CTG on the baby straight away and then examine her.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Her pain is in the right iliac fossa. What next?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's clearly appendicitis, the signs are typical.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A CT abdomen, it's the most accurate.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: MRI shows an inflamed appendix. How do you manage it?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd give antibiotics and try to hold off surgery until she has delivered.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It would have to be open. Laparoscopy isn't safe in pregnancy.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd tell obstetrics after the operation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ABCDE for her first, in left lateral tilt. IV access, fluids, analgesia and an antiemetic, and I'd call obstetrics early.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Appendicitis, but signs are less reliable in pregnancy. I'd consider pyelonephritis, ovarian torsion, abruption and preterm labour, and send urine and bloods.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Graded compression ultrasound first. If it's inconclusive, MRI.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: MRI shows acute appendicitis. What now?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: She needs an appendicectomy without delay. Antibiotics alone aren't recommended in pregnancy.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Laparoscopic is safe in any trimester if we have the expertise. Left lateral tilt, and I'd place the first port according to the fundal height.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the risks to the baby?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Miscarriage and preterm delivery, both more likely if the appendix perforates.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Obstetrics and anaesthetics. At 20 weeks the baby isn't yet viable, so obstetrics document the fetal heart with a Doppler before and after surgery, and I'd include the pregnancy risks in her consent.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Resuscitating her is the best thing for the baby. Lying flat, the uterus compresses the vena cava, so I'd keep her tilted to the left.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Less so in pregnancy: white cell count and nausea are often raised anyway. I'd image her rather than rely on a score.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then CT is acceptable if the result will change management. I'd discuss it with the radiologist rather than delay.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The ultrasound was equivocal and she's settling.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A short period of in-hospital observation with repeat ultrasound is reasonable. But I wouldn't let her drift towards perforation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd keep the pneumoperitoneum at 10 to 15 millimetres of mercury, adjusted to her physiology, with calf compression and early mobilisation.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Can you put numbers on the fetal risk?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In one large series, fetal loss was about 2% with simple appendicitis, 6% with complicated, and 4% with a negative appendicectomy. So we need an accurate diagnosis both ways.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not prophylactically. Obstetrics would treat signs of preterm labour if they appear. I'd involve my consultant and document the joint plan.

failures.consequence: Safety-critical: risks perforation, maternal sepsis and fetal loss.

failures.move: Requesting CT first-line without trying ultrasound.
failures.consequence: Unnecessary fetal radiation when ultrasound and MRI can answer the question.

failures.move: Unable to explain the risks to the pregnancy.
failures.consequence: Cannot consent her properly or justify timely surgery.

failures.move: Leaving her supine and focusing on the fetus.
failures.consequence: Caval compression and maternal hypotension harm both mother and fetus.

recovery.when: Asked whether pregnancy changes the urgency
recovery.line: It doesn't delay surgery: the risk to the baby comes mainly from perforation.
Ultrasound, then MRI; CT if it's needed and MRI isn't available.

knowledge.fact: Imaging: graded compression ultrasound first; MRI if inconclusive; don't diagnose on symptoms and signs alone.
Non-operative treatment is not recommended in pregnancy; laparoscopic appendicectomy is preferred when surgery is indicated.
Laparoscopy is safe in any trimester; left lateral tilt after the first trimester; entry adjusted to fundal height; CO2 at 10–15 mmHg.
Fetal loss: about 2% simple, 4% negative, 6% complicated appendicitis.

recall.think: Perforation and maternal sepsis threaten both lives.
do: ABCDE in left lateral tilt; call obstetrics

numbers.meaning: fetal loss, simple vs complicated appendicitis

recall.trap: Treating with antibiotics to buy time until delivery.
recall.finish: Laparoscopic appendicectomy with obstetric and anaesthetic support; fetal heart documented (Doppler) before and after.

sources.name: Di Saverio S, Podda M, De Simone B, et al. Diagnosis and treatment of acute appendicitis: 2020 update of the WSES Jerusalem guidelines. World J Emerg Surg 2020;15:27
sources.supports: Pregnancy: do not diagnose on symptoms and signs alone; clinical scores less accurate; graded compression ultrasound first; MRI after inconclusive ultrasound if available; short in-hospital observation with repeat ultrasound acceptable when equivocal; against non-operative treatment in pregnancy; laparoscopic appendicectomy preferred to open

sources.name: Pearl JP, Price RR, Tonkin AE, Richardson WS, Stefanidis D. SAGES guidelines for the use of laparoscopy during pregnancy. Surg Endosc 2017;31:3767–82
sources.supports: Laparoscopy safe in any trimester; left lateral decubitus beyond the first trimester to avoid caval compression; entry adjusted to fundal height; CO2 10–15 mmHg adjusted to physiology; fetal heart rate monitoring before and after urgent surgery for a viable fetus, lower limit of viability 22 to 24 weeks (guideline 21); mechanical VTE prophylaxis and early ambulation; no prophylactic tocolytics; ultrasound first, MRI preferred to CT; CT may be used in emergency situations but should not be the initial imaging test (guideline 3)

sources.name: McGory ML, Zingmond DS, Tillou A, et al. Negative appendectomy in pregnant women is associated with a substantial risk of fetal loss. J Am Coll Surg 2007;205:534–40
sources.supports: Fetal loss 2% simple, 4% negative and 6% complicated appendicitis in 3,133 pregnant women

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

media.task: Recognise an inflamed appendix on MRI in a pregnant patient
media.description: Axial or coronal T2 MRI at about 20 weeks' gestation showing a thickened, fluid-filled appendix with periappendiceal fluid, and the gravid uterus

partner.opening: Mrs Kershaw is 20 weeks pregnant with right-sided pain and fever. How would you approach her?

reveals.finding: HR 108, BP 112/68, RR 20, SpO2 98% on air, temperature 38.1°C. Tender right flank and right iliac fossa.
WCC 16, CRP 98. Urine dipstick: trace leucocytes, nitrite negative. No vaginal bleeding.
Appendix not seen. Small amount of free fluid in the right iliac fossa. Fetal heart present.
Thickened, fluid-filled appendix with surrounding inflammation. No abscess.

push.question: Why not rely on examination?
push.expect: Signs and scores less reliable in pregnancy; imaging needed.

push.question: Could you treat her with antibiotics?
push.expect: Not recommended in pregnancy; appendicectomy without delay.

push.question: Is laparoscopy safe?
push.expect: Yes, any trimester; tilt, fundal-height entry, 10–15 mmHg.

push.question: What are the risks to the baby?
push.expect: Fetal loss and preterm delivery, higher with perforation.

curveballs.prompt: She asks whether the operation could make her miscarry.
curveballs.safeAnswer: There is a small risk, but it is higher if the appendix perforates; the obstetric team will check the baby before and after.

curveballs.prompt: MRI isn't available until tomorrow and she looks septic.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Don't wait: CT if it will change management, or proceed to surgery on clinical grounds with senior input.

curveballs.prompt: She starts having regular tightenings after surgery.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Urgent obstetric review; tocolysis is their decision, not prophylactic.
